newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ hauls EU before world trade body over butter.
newsitem.headline: NZ hauls EU before world trade body over butter.

text.p: New Zealand said on Monday it was turning to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to break the deadlock in a dispute over exports of spreadable butter to the European Union.

New Zealand, a major dairy and wool exporting nation, has previously supported other countries in similar moves, but it was the first time it had brought a case of its own before the global trade body.
The dispute arose from exports of a soft New Zealand butter, manufactured by a process called AMMIX, which is easier to spread than traditional butter.
The EU last year excluded such butter from eligibility for reduced duties under New Zealand's 76,000 tonne quota for butter exports to the 15-nation group.
"The EU's decision is a clear breach of the obligations which it owes New Zealand under the WTO agreement," New Zealand Trade Minister Lockwood Smith said.
"We have made intensive efforts to resolve this issue through bilateral contacts. I regret that these have failed to break the impasse between New Zealand and the EU."

The AMMIX process differs from traditional methods of making butter, in that it splits the cream into fat and fluid. The fat can in turn be divided into hard and soft fractions, and the latter used to make a butter that is easier to spread.
New Zealand disputes the EU's contention that the spreadable butter is not made directly from milk or cream.
A trade official said that but for the EU move, New Zealand planned to export 6,000 tonnes of spreadable butter to the EU this year.

A spokesman for the New Zealand Dairy Board, the world's biggest multinational dairy marketing group, said the cost of making the spreadable butter in Europe to avoid the higher duties was about NZ$10 million (US$6.94 million) a year.

"But the fact is we've spent about $75 million investing in plant, equipment, packaging, advertising, promotion and all of that for this product, and that is jeopardised by this action," spokesman Neville Martin said.
He said the product was strategically important because it was winning young consumers and growing the overall market for butter, to the benefit of all manufacturers.
Under WTO rules, New Zealand and the EU now have 60 further days for consultation. Officials said this was the first stage in a process leading to the convening of a WTO panel to rule on the dispute.
